facts.statement: The genus Paracestracion was first described in 1911 by Ernst Hermann Friedrich von Koken in Karl Alfred von Zittel.
facts.quote: The genus was first described in 1911 by Ernst Hermann Friedrich von Koken in Karl Alfred von Zittel.

facts.statement: Paracestracion lived from the Early Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous in rocks found in England, France, Germany, and Luxembourg.
facts.quote: Paracestracion is an extinct genus of heterodontiform sharks from Early Jurassic to Early Cretaceous-aged rocks of England, France, Germany and Luxembourg.

facts.statement: Well-preserved full body fossils show that Paracestracion differed from living bullhead sharks by having a shorter skull and different placements for the pelvic girdle and fins.
facts.quote: The genus contains several Late Jurassic species known from well preserved full body remains, which show that it differs from the living bullhead sharks in the placement of the pelvic girdle and fins, as well as by having a shorter skull.

facts.statement: Recent studies have classified Paracestracion into its own family, Paracestracionidae.
facts.quote: Recent studies have classified it into its own family, Paracestracionidae.

facts.statement: The parent group of Paracestracion is the family Heterodontidae.
Paracestracion lived between 184.2 and 132.6 million years ago, from the Toarcian to the Valanginian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Toarcian to Valanginian (184.2 to 132.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: The genus includes up to six species, including P. bellis from England, the type species P. falcifer from England and Germany, P. sarstedtensis and P. viohli from Germany, and an indeterminate species from Luxembourg.
facts.quote: At maximum, the genus contains five species: P. bellis from the Bathonian of England, the type species P. falcifer from the Tithonian and Kimmeridgian of Weymouth, England and Solnhofen, Germany, which was originally named as a species of Cestracion (now seen as a synonym of Heterodontus) in 1857 by Johann Andreas Wagner, P. sarstedtensis, originally classified as a species of Heterodontus, from the Toarcian and Aalenian of Germany, and P. viohli from the Tithonian-aged Painten Formation of Germany, with a sixth indeterminate species known from the Toarcian-aged Variabilis layer of the La Couche à Crassum (part of the larger Posidonia Shale) of Luxembourg.

facts.statement: The species P. pectinatus from the Early Cretaceous of France is known only from isolated teeth.
facts.quote: P. pectinatus from the Early Cretaceous (Valanginian) of France has been described on the basis of isolated teeth.
